case_name: Section 1 of the Owners, Strata Plan LMS 2643 v. Harold Developments Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Section 1 of the Owners, Strata Plan LMS 2643 v. Harold
Developments Ltd.,

2007 BCSC 1095

Date: 20070723

Docket:
L052627

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Section
1 of the Owners, Strata Plan LMS 2643

Plaintiff

And

Harold
Developments Ltd., James Kwan, Yvonne Kwan,

William Kwan, and others

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Sigurdson

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.G.
Mendes

P.G. Mendes

Counsel for the
Defendants, Harold Developments Ltd., James Kwan, and Yvonne Kwan:

T.
Yu

Date and Place of Hearing:

April
5, 2007

Vancouver,
B.C.

NATURE
OF APPLICATION

[
1
]

The plaintiff, Section 1 of the Owners, Strata
Plan LMS 2643, seeks damages for the alleged defective construction of a condominium
called “Lighthouse Place”.  This claim involves what has become known as a
leaky condo.

[
2
]

In this application, the plaintiff seeks to
amend its statement of claim to provide particulars of its claim for damages
for negligence and a duty to warn against James Kwan and Yvonne Kwan, who are
the sole directors of Harold Developments Ltd., the contractor which provided
labour and materials in respect of the design and construction of the
condominium.  The evidence shows that at one point, James Kwan and Yvonne Kwan
owned 43 of the 106 condominium units.

[
3
]

The defendants, James Kwan and Yvonne Kwan, had
earlier filed an application to strike out the existing pleadings against them
in the original statement of claim on the ground that they disclosed no reasonable
cause of action.  They also take the position that there is no reasonable cause
of action disclosed by the further proposed amendments that the plaintiff seeks
to make to the statement of claim.  They also assert that the proposed
amendments should not be allowed because the claim is statute-barred by reason
of the
Limitation Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266.

[
4
]

The defendants say that in order to establish a
cause of action against an employee or director of a corporation, a plaintiff
must show that the individual committed a tortious act which demonstrated an
identity or interest that was separate from that of the company.

[
5
]

The plaintiff says that the amendments ought to
be allowed because it is not plain and obvious that there cannot be personal
liability for employees or directors of a company unless the alleged actions
are tortious
and
exhibit a separate identity.  The plaintiff submits
that the law in this area is unsettled and, as such, it is not plain and
obvious that the claim that is proposed by the amendments cannot succeed, and
argues that the amended claim should go to trial where the legal issue can be
determined, not in a vacuum, but in a complete factual setting.

[
6
]

Moreover, the plaintiff says that the proposed
amendments are not out of time, as they simply particularize a claim in
negligence that already appears in the statement of claim.  The plaintiff says
that the claim of negligence in the statement of claim was simply an
alteration, modification, or extension of the claim against the Kwans in the
writ issued on November 2, 2005 and was permitted under Rule 20(3).  Even if
the proposed amendments allege a cause of action that might be out of time,
which the plaintiff disputes, the plaintiff says that the joinder of a cause of
action outside the limitation period should be permitted and the limitation
period is simply one factor to be considered in deciding whether to allow the
amendment.

[
7
]

Let me set out the pleadings from the initial
writ, which was issued on November 2, 2005; the statement of claim of March 13,
2006; and further proposed amended statement of claim attached to the notice of
motion dated October 27, 2006.  Further proposed revisions to the statement of
claim were described in the plaintiff’s March 15, 2007 outline.

[
8
]

The writ of summons names a number of defendants
including the Kwans.  Insofar as the Kwans are concerned, the writ alleges a
breach of a duty to warn.  The endorsement in the writ as it relates to the
Kwans reads, in part:

The Plaintiff and the Owners claim general
damages, special damages, interest and costs against the Defendants as a result
of defects in the workmanship, materials and design of the strata lots, common
property, common facilities, and other assets of the Strata Corporation (the
“Construction Deficiencies”) comprising the condominium building located at
5860 Dover Crescent, Richmond, British Columbia and known as “Lighthouse Place”
(the “Condominium”).

…

The Construction Deficiencies were caused or
contributed to by the negligence of the following Defendants, who breached
their duty of care to the Plaintiff and Owners:

… [a number of individual defendants are
mentioned, but they do not include the Kwans]

Each of the Defendants breached its duty to the
Plaintiff and Owners to warn of the Construction Deficiencies.

…

The Disclosure Statement contains material
false statements for which Harold Developments Ltd., James Kwan, Yvonne Kwan
and William Kwan are liable under section 75 of the
Real Estate Act
and
section 22 of the
Real Estate Development Marketing Act
, as amended, and
at common law.  …

…

The Strata Corporation and the Owners have
suffered and continue to suffer loss, damage and resultant damage as a result
of the Construction Deficiencies and the aforementioned breaches of contract,
breaches of duty of care, breaches of duty to warn and material false
statements.  This loss, damage and resultant damage includes:

1.         the cost of investigating and repairing the Construction
Deficiencies;

2.         the cost of investigating and repairing resultant damage
to the strata lots, common property, common facilities and other assets of the
Plaintiff and the Owners;

3.         depreciation in the market value of the strata lots,
common property, common facilities and other assets of the Plaintiff and the
Owners; and

4.         increased
property management costs.

[
9
]

The statement of claim filed March 13, 2006
contained allegations against the individual defendants, the Kwans, extended
negligence claims against them and particularized the claim with respect to the
disclosure obligation under the
Real Estate Act
, (which is not
the subject of this application).  It contained the following paragraphs:

70.       At
all material times, the Defendants owed the Strata Corporation and the Owners a
duty of care to take all reasonable steps to ensure that the construction of
the Condominium complied with the
British Columbia Building Code
and the
City’s bylaws, that the Condominium was:

a.         designed in accordance with prudent design principles;

b.         built in a good and workmanlike manner in accordance with
prudent construction practices; and

c.         built with
suitable materials, and would be fit for its purpose, namely, habitation.

…

74.       Further,
or in the alternative, the Defendants and each of them, owed the Strata
Corporation and the Owners a duty to warn of the Construction Deficiencies.

75.       The
Defendants breached the foregoing duties to the Strata Corporation and the
Owners.

76.
The Defendants’ breaches of duty caused or contributed to the
Construction Deficiencies, the Resultant Damage and the Dangerous Defects.

77.       The
Defendants are jointly and severally liable for the loss and damage suffered by
the Strata Corporation and the Owners, and the Strata Corporation specifically
pleads and relies upon the
Negligence Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 333,
and amendments thereto.

[
10
]

The application to amend the statement of claim
that is before me on this application contained the following proposed
amendments as underlined below.

8.         Harold
Developments
James Kwan, Yvonne Kwan and William Kwan were
the
developer
of the Condominium
and a contractor that provided labour or materials in
respect of the design and construction of the Condominium.  James Kwan, Yvonne
Kwan and William Kwan were at all material times directors and officers of
Harold Developments.

…

70.       At
all material times, the Defendants
and each of them
owed the Strata
Corporation and the Owners a duty of care to take all reasonable steps to
ensure that the construction of the Condominium complied with the
British
Columbia Building Code
and the City’s bylaws, that the Condominium was:

a.         designed in accordance with prudent design principles;

b.         built in a good and workmanlike manner in accordance with
prudent construction practices; and

c.         built with suitable materials, and would be fit for its
purpose, namely, habitation.

71.       Harold
Developments
as the developer and builder of the Condominium, and James
Kwan, Yvonne Kwan and William Kwan as the principals and directing minds of
Harold Developments
further owed the Strata Corporation and the Owners a duty
of care to use all due care, skill, diligence and competence:

a.
to select consultants, contractors and suppliers
during the design and construction of Condominium that were qualified and
experienced in multi-family residential construction
;

b.
to ensure the design of the Condominium was not
defective and complied with all specifications, industry standards, building
codes and statutory requirements including the
British Columbia Building
Code
and the City’s bylaws
;

c.         to ensure the work and materials of contractors,
suppliers, consultants and workers under its direction or control
was not
defective and
complied with all specifications, industry standards,
building codes and statutory requirements including the
British Columbia
Building Code
and the City’s bylaws;

d.

to ensure the Condominium
would be fit for its intended use of habitation; and

e.

to ensure the Condominium
would not pose a risk to the health and safety of its occupants.

…

74.       Further,
or in the alternative, the Defendants
and each of them
owed the Strata
Corporation and the Owners a duty to warn of the Construction Deficiencies.

75.
The Defendants
and each of them
breached the foregoing duties to
the Strata Corporation and the Owners.

75.1

James Kwan, Yvonne Kwan and
William Kwan breached the duty of care owed to the Strata Corporation and the
Owners by failing to exercise the standard of care required of a reasonably
prudent person in the circumstances:

a.

failing to select
consultants, contractors and suppliers during the design and construction of
Condominium that were qualified and experienced in multi-family residential
construction;

b.

failing to ensure that the
design of the Condominium was not defective and complied with all
specifications, industry standards, building codes and statutory requirements
including the
British Columbia Building Code
and the City’s bylaws

c.

failing to ensure the work
and materials of contractors, suppliers, consultants and workers under its
direction or control was not defective and complied with all specifications,
industry standards, building codes and statutory requirements including the
British
Columbia Building Code
and the City’s bylaws;

d.

failing to ensure that the
Condominium would be fit for its intended use of habitation; and

e.

failing to ensure that the
Condominium would not pose a risk to the health and safety of its occupants.

76A.    The
Defendants’ breaches of duty caused or contributed to the Construction
Deficiencies, the Resultant Damage and the Dangerous Defects.  In particular:

a.         Harold Developments’
James Kwan, Yvonne Kwan and
William Kwan
breach of duty caused or contributed to the Construction
Deficiencies set out in subparagraphs 45(a), 45(b), and 45(c)(i) to (xvii);

…

77.       The
Defendants are jointly and severally liable for the loss and damage suffered by
the Strata Corporation and the Owners, and the Strata Corporation specifically
pleads and relies upon the
Negligence Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 333, and
amendments thereto.

[emphasis in original]

[
11
]

This case is set for trial in October 2008.

[
12
]

In summary and in general terms, the writ of
summons contained a claim against the individual defendant Kwans of a duty to
warn of construction deficiencies.  The statement of claim contained
allegations of negligence and a duty to warn against the defendant Kwans.  The
proposed amended statement of claim, the subject of this application, contains
particulars of the defendant Kwans’ alleged duty of care and breach of the
alleged duty of care.

[
13
]

In
Langret Investments S.A. v. McDonnell
(1996),

1996 CanLII 1433 (BC CA)
, 21 B.C.L.R. (3d) 145 (C.A.), Rowles J.A. said at ¶34:

Rule 24(1) of the
Rules of Court in British Columbia allows a party to amend an originating
process or pleading.  Amendments are allowed unless prejudice can be
demonstrated by the opposite party or the amendment will be
useless.  The rationale for allowing amendments is to enable the real
issues to be determined.  The practice followed in civil matters when
amendments are sought fulfils the fundamental objective of the civil rules which
is to ensure the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every proceeding
on the merits.  See McLachlin and Taylor, British Columbia Practice
(2nd Ed.) pp. 24-1 to 24-2-10, and the decision of this Court in Chavez v.
Sundance Cruises Corp. (1993),
1993 CanLII 2432 (BC CA)
, 15 C.P.C. (3d) 305, 309-10.

[
14
]

An amendment will be refused if it is plain and
obvious as a matter of law or fact that the amendment does not disclose a cause
of action:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959.  If
there is any doubt, it should be resolved in favour of permitting the pleadings
to stand:
McGauley v. British Columbia
(1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d)
223 (C.A.);
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) at ¶34.

[
15
]

In
Carley Estate v. Allied Signal Inc.

(1997),
1997 CanLII 2870 (BC CA)
, 35 B.C.L.R. (3d) 54 (C.A.) Lambert J.A. said at ¶3:

… The test that is to be applied is summarized
by Madam Justice McLachlin in
McNaughton v. Baker
(1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25
B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (B.C.C.A.).  Madam Justice McLachlin said this:

Before the courts will strike out a
pleading or refuse an amendment on the ground that it discloses no reasonable
cause of action or defence the case must be perfectly clear.  In
Minnes
v. Minnes
, (1962),
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.), it was stated that the
power to strike out a pleading on the ground that it discloses no reasonable
cause of action "should be exercised only where the case is absolutely
beyond doubt."

[
16
]

The defendants’ position is that it is settled
law that to establish a cause of action against an employee or a director of a
company, the plaintiff must show that the individual committed a tortious act
which demonstrated an identity or interest separate from that of the company.

[
17
]

The defendants cite a number of authorities that
support their proposition including
Steele v. Riverside Forest Products
Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 1598
;
Strata Plan LMS 1965 v. 450526 B.C. Ltd.
,

2002 BCSC 155
; and
Rafiki Properties Ltd. v. Integrated Housing
Development Ltd.
(1999),
1999 CanLII 6389 (BC SC)
, 45 B.L.R. (2d) 316 (S.C.).

[
18
]

In
Strata Plan LMS 1965 v. 450526 B.C.
Ltd.
, Allan J. heard an application to join further defendants who
allegedly caused or contributed to deficiencies in the design and construction
of a townhouse complex that resulted in alleged leaks and building envelope
deficiencies.  The factual circumstances have some similarity to this case.
The individuals sought to be joined were described in the proposed pleadings as
officers or key employees acting within the scope of their duties and limits of
authority as employees of various defendant companies.  Allan J. said at
¶15-17:

[15]      The development of the law of
personal liability of directors of corporations was canvassed by the Ontario
Court of Appeal in
ADGA Systems International Ltd. v. Valcom Ltd.

(1999),
1999 CanLII 1527 (ON CA)
, 43 O.R. (3d) 101, leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused, [1999] S.C.C.A.
No. 124 at p. 105:

That beginning is found in the House of
Lords' decision in
Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
, [1895-9]
All E.R. 33 (H.L.), which established that a company, once legally
incorporated, must be treated like any other independent person, with rights
and liabilities appropriate to itself.  From time to time, litigants have
sought to lift this "corporate veil", by seeking to make principals
of the corporation liable for the obligations of the corporation.  However,
where, as here, the plaintiff relies upon establishing an independent cause of
action against the principals of the company, the corporate veil is not
threatened and the Salomon principle remains intact.

In
ADGA
, Carthy J.A. cited
Montreal
Trust Co. of Canada v. ScotiaMcLeod Inc.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 1301 (ON CA)
, 129 D.L.R. (4th) 711
(Ont. C.A.), at p. 112:

... officers or employees of limited
companies are protected from personal liability unless it can be shown that
their actions are themselves tortious or exhibit a separate identity or interest
from that of the company so as to make the act or conduct complained of their
own.

[16]      In this case, the particulars of
negligence alleged against Naudi, Hildebrandt and McDonald do not distinguish
between their actions or omissions, if any, as employees, and those of their
companies.  The construction services that they are alleged to have provided
negligently were the same services undertaken by their companies.  No
independent cause of action is pled against them, nor is there evidence to
support any allegation that they were negligent.

[17]      As
Clancy J. stated in
Rafiki
at para. 17, "To fix the
principals with personal liability there must be an independent cause of action
alleged."  Such an independent cause of action existed in
Lasik
Vision Canada Inc. v. TLC Vancouver Optometric Group Inc. and Michael Melenchuk

(1999),
1999 CanLII 1002 (BC SC)
, 37 C.P.C. (4th) 380 (B.C.S.C.).  There, Mr. Justice Macaulay
permitted the plaintiff to add personal defendants where the plaintiff made
allegations of malicious defamation against the proposed defendants.  Those
allegations constituted a cause of action against the principals separate from
that against the company.  Macaulay J. noted that if such allegations were
proven, the individuals may not be protected by the corporate veil.

[
19
]

Allan J. went on to say at ¶20:

[20]      The issue of personal liability was
recently discussed in
Blacklaws v. Morrow
, (2000)
2000 ABCA 175 (CanLII)
, 84 Alta. L.R.
(3d) 270; 2000 ABCA 175.  There, the Alberta Court of Appeal acknowledged, at
para. 41, that:

... there will be circumstances in which
the actions of a shareholder, officer, director or employee of a corporation
may give rise to personal liability in tort despite the fact that the impugned
acts were ones performed in the course of their duties to the corporation.
Where those actions are themselves tortious or exhibit a separate identity or
interest from that of the corporation so as to make the act or conduct
complained of their own, they may well attract personal liability.

[
20
]

In the case at bar, the plaintiff does not
distinguish in the particulars of negligence between the actions of the Kwans
and the company.  The Kwans’ alleged failure to exercise the standard of care
required of a reasonably prudent person in selecting consultants, ensuring
materials were not defective, ensuring the design was not defective and
ensuring that the condominium was fit for the intended use and would not pose a
health risk are the same allegations that are made against the company.  There
is no independent tort pleaded against the directors.

[
21
]

The defendants also referred to
Jam's
International Ventures Ltd. v. Westbank Holdings Ltd.
,
2003 BCCA 232
, a
case where leave to appeal was denied from a decision refusing to add the
principal of a corporate defendant under the allegation of negligence and misrepresentation.
That case was followed in
Link v. Texas Oil & Gas Inc.
,
2006
BCSC 1520
, which dismissed an application to add an individual defendant who
was president of the corporate defendant to an action for breach of contract.
Bruce J. said at ¶31: “… there is an obligation to identify what [the
president] did or did not do outside of his role as the directing mind and
alter ego of the company that gives rise to the alleged cause of action”.

[
22
]

While the plaintiff’s counsel acknowledges that
he is unable to distinguish
Jam’s
and
Rafiki
, he
says that there is authority that points in the opposite direction, and that as
such it is not plain and obvious that there is not a cause of action and
therefore the amendments ought to be allowed.

[
23
]

The plaintiffs refer to the decision of Madam
Justice Garson in
Strata Plan LMS 2262 v. Stoneman Developments Ltd.
,

2004 BCSC 828
, in which she referred to the decision of Melnick J. in
Glenayre
Manufacturing Ltd. v. Pilot Pacific Properties Inc.
, [2003] B.C.J. No.
456,
2003 BCSC 303
, leave to appeal refused [2003] B.C.J. No. 2034,
2003 BCCA
462
, [2004] B.C.J. No. 302, 2004 BCCA 54.
Stoneman
was a
building envelope claim in which the plaintiff strata corporation applied to
join Mr. Stoneman, a director of the defendant developers.

[
24
]

The allegation against Mr. Stoneman in his
personal capacity was that he was the president of the contractor and at all
material times was a “developer of and contractor for Carnarvon Towers and was
personally responsible for, participated in, and supervised the design,
development, and construction of Carnarvon Towers”.  Garson J. said that the
plaintiffs had provided no evidence demonstrating that Mr. Stoneman’s
actions were independent from his duties as his company’s principal or that he
was operating under an identity or interest separate from that of the
company.   However, Garson J., who ultimately did not join Mr. Stoneman,
because it was not just and convenient to do so, did not conclude that it was
plain and obvious that there was no cause of action.  She said, at ¶85-92:

[85}     In British Columbia there are two
conflicting lines of authority relating to the independent liability of
corporate employees acting within the scope of their employment.

[86]      One line of authority holds that an
employee is not personally liable unless his actions are themselves tortious
and exhibit a separate identity or interest from that of the company.  (
Strata
Plan LMS 1965 v. 450526 B.C. Ltd.
, [2002] B.C.J. No. 407,
2002 BCSC
155
;
Rafiki Properties Ltd. v. Integrated Housing Development Ltd.

(1999),

1999 CanLII 6389 (BC SC)
, 45 B.L.R. (2d) 316 (S.C.);
Jam's International Venture Ltd. v. Westbank
Holdings Ltd.
, [2003] B.C.J. No. 891,
2003 BCCA 232
.)

[87]      The opposite line of authority holds
that an independent tort is not required, and that an employee or director may
be sued personally if his actions are tortious or exhibit a separate identity
or interest from that of the company.  (
Glenayre Manufacturing Ltd. v.
Pilot Pacific Properties Inc.
, [2003] B.C.J. No. 456,
2003 BCSC 303
, leave
to appeal refused [2003] B.C.J. No. 2034,
2003 BCCA 462
, [2004] B.C.J. No. 302,
2004 BCCA 54.)

[88]      Mr. Peters for Mr. Stoneman argues
that the Court of Appeal in
Jam's
puts to rest the question of
whether liability can be visited on officers and employees of limited companies
where their actions may be tortious but not otherwise exhibiting a separate
identity or interest from that of the company so as to make the act or conduct
complained of their own.  He argues that, while the evidentiary threshold is
low, there must be some evidence that supports the allegation that the intended
party, an officer and director of the corporate defendant, acted independently
from his role as principal of, and agent for, the corporate body.

[89]      Melnick J. in
Glenayre
found
support for the proposition that no independent tort was required in the
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
London Drugs Ltd. v. Kuehne
& Nagel International Ltd.
(1992),
1992 CanLII 41 (SCC)
, 73 B.C.L.R. (2d) 1 (S.C.C.). In
London Drugs Iacobucci J. stated at ¶185 that:

There is no general rule in Canada to the
effect that an employee acting in the course of his or her employment and
performing the "very essence" of his or her employer's contractual
obligations with a customer does not owe a duty of care, whether one labels it
"independent" or otherwise, to the employer's customer.  Our law of
negligence has long since moved away from a category approach when dealing with
duties of care. It is now well established that the question of whether a duty
of care arises will depend on the circumstances of each particular case, not on
pre-determined categories and blanket rules as to who is, and who is not, under
a duty to exercise reasonable care.

[90]      Leave to appeal Melnick J.'s decision
in
Glenayre
was denied by a single judge of the Court of Appeal,
apparently on the basis that, since the law on the separate liability of
corporate directors was uncertain, the argument that it was plain and obvious
that the claims could not succeed had little prospect of success at appeal,
[2003] B.C.J. No. 1421,
2003 BCCA 363
(¶11).  A three-judge panel at the Court
of Appeal found that, since there were no errors or misconceptions of fact made
by the single justice at the leave application, the panel could not intervene,

2003 BCCA 462
.

[91]      Leave to appeal in
Glenayre
,
denied by the three-judge panel, was on August 14, 2003, several months after
the court's decision in
Jam's
.  It could be said that Jam's was
not a considered decision in the sense that counsel before the chambers judge,
Baker J. and then again before Levine J.A. appear to have conceded the
necessity of an independent tort.

[92]      In the
result, I conclude that the law in British Columbia is not settled on this
point, and therefore there may be an issue to be determined between the
plaintiffs and Mr. Stoneman which is all that is required to meet the threshold
test under Rule 15(5)(a)(iii).

[
25
]

In
Glenayre
, Melnick J. referred
to
Strata Plan LMS 1965

and
Rafiki Properties Ltd.
,
two of the cases referred to by the defendants, and said at ¶34-35 and ¶43:

[34]      However, Madam Justice Allan in
Strata Plan LMS
1965

did refer to
London Drugs
,
Rafiki
,
ADGA

and
ScotiaMcLeod
.  She concluded that, in the
circumstances before her,
London Drugs
did not assist the
plaintiff as no reasonable cause of action had been pleaded against the
proposed plaintiffs and no evidence had been adduced to support a separate
cause of action against them personally.  She noted at para. 16 that, in the
case before her, the particulars of negligence alleged against the proposed
defendants did not distinguish between their actions or omissions, if any, as
employees and those of their companies.  However, she also referred to the
decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal in
Blacklaws v. Morrow

(2000),

2000 ABCA 175 (CanLII)
, 84 Alta. L.R. (3d) 270; 2000 ABCA 175.  She noted that the Alberta Court of
Appeal had:

... acknowledged, at para. 41, that:

... there will be circumstances in which the actions of a
shareholder, officer, director or employee of a corporation may give rise to
personal liability in tort despite the fact that the impugned acts were ones
performed in the course of their duties to the corporation.  Where those
actions are themselves tortious or exhibit a separate identity or interest from
that of the corporation so as to make the act or conduct complained of their
own, they may well attract personal liability.

[35]      I note that these words of the Alberta Court of Appeal
mirror those in
ScotiaMcLeod
.

…

[43]      To
return to the "or test" and the "and test", I conclude that
the thrust of the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada in
London
Drugs
and
Edgeworth
are more in keeping with the test
articulated by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
ScotiaMcLeod
and
ADGA

than by Mr. Justice Clancy in
Rafiki
.  That being
the case, and not overlooking the limitations placed on me by
Hansard
Spruce Mills
, I conclude that to the extent the difference in the
wording may be of significance on how I view the adequacy of Glenayre's
proposed pleadings, I will apply the "or test" from
ScotiaMcLeod

as approved in
ADGA
.

[
26
]

I have concluded that, given the uncertain state
of the law on a director’s liability when the alleged tortious acts are ones
that the director performed in the course of his duties to the company, I am
unable to say that it is plain and obvious that there is no cause of action.
The liability of the Kwans will have to be decided at trial when all of the
facts are known.

[
27
]

As I am unable to conclude that it is plain and
obvious that the claim will fail, the amendments cannot be denied on that basis.

[
28
]

The Kwans however say that the amendment should
not be allowed because of the
Limitation Act
.  They say that the
plaintiffs are adding new causes of action after the expiration of the
limitation period and the writ did not include a claim against the Kwans in
negligence.

[
29
]

The evidence concerning a possible limitation
defence is in issue, but is as follows.  The construction was apparently done
in 1995 and 1996 with an occupancy permit issued to the developer on December
20, 1996.  The defendants contend that the plaintiffs knew of the leaks from
1997 and that the strata corporation retained an expert and obtained a report
in July 2000.  The action was started on November 2, 2005 and the statement of
claim was filed on March 13, 2006.  The defendants say that at the latest the
limitation period expired six years after July 2000 and, therefore, the claim
as particularized against the individual Kwans in October 2006, when these
proposed pleadings were tendered, is months out of time.  The plaintiff argues
that the limitation date probably did not begin to run until December 2000,
when the expert’s report was presented to the owner (
Strata Plan No. VR
1720 v. Bart Developments Ltd.
(1998),
1998 CanLII 6569 (BC SC)
, 53 B.C.L.R. (3d) 289 (S.C.),
aff’d
1999 BCCA 585
).

[
30
]

Section 4(4) of the
Limitation Act

states as follows:

In any action the
court may allow the amendment of a pleading, on terms as to costs or otherwise
that the court considers just, even if between the issue of the writ and the
application for amendment a fresh cause of action disclosed by the amendment
would have become barred by the lapse of time

[
31
]

In
Teal Cedar Products (1977) Ltd. v. Dale
Intermediaries Ltd.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 3033 (BC CA)
, 19 B.C.L.R. (3d) 282 (C.A.), Finch J.A. as
he then was said:

[45]      On
principle, therefore, it appears to me that the discretion to permit amendments
afforded by both Rule 24(1) and s. 4(4) of the [
Limitation
]

Act
was intended to be completely unfettered and subject only to the
general rule that all such discretion is to be exercised judicially, in
accordance with the evidence adduced and such guidelines as may appear from the
authorities.  Delay, and the reasons for delay, are among the
relevant considerations, and the judge should consider any explanation put
forward to account for the delay.  But no one factor should be
accorded overriding importance, in the absence of a clear evidentiary basis for
doing so.

[
32
]

He went on to say at ¶67:

[67]      In the
exercise of a judge's discretion, the length of delay, the reasons for delay
and the expiry of the limitation period are all factors to be considered, but
none of those factors should be considered in isolation.  Regard must also be
had for the presence or absence of prejudice, and the extent of the connection,
if any, between the existing claims and the proposed new cause of action.  …

[
33
]

The plaintiff says that the issue of a possible
limitation defence does not really arise.  The plaintiff says that the
endorsement in the writ sets out sufficient facts to support a claim in
negligence against the Kwans, or, if not, then the pleading of negligence in
the statement of claim is a permissible extension without amending the writ.

[
34
]

Rule 20(3) provides:

The plaintiff may,
in a statement of claim, alter, modify or extend the claim without amending the
endorsement on the writ.

[
35
]

In the endorsement to the writ, the plaintiff
claims damages in connection with the defects in the workmanship, materials,
and design of the strata lots comprising the condominium (defined as the
Construction Deficiencies) and says that “[e]ach of the Defendants breached its
duty to the Plaintiff and Owners to warn of the Construction Deficiencies”.
Although the defendants say that the endorsement in the original writ did not
include a claim in negligence against the Kwans, as the statement of claim does,
the plaintiff’s argument is that the proposed amendments are not of a character
that is entirely different from that of the claims in the endorsement, and thus
fall within Rule 20(3).

[
36
]

The plaintiff says that the inclusion of a
negligence claim against the Kwans in the original statement of claim of March
13, 2006 was, as allowed by Rule 20(3), an alteration, modification, or
extension of the breach of duty to warn claim against them in the writ.  The
plaintiff refers to
Wells Cartage Ltd. v. Goodyear Aerospace Corp.

(1987),
1987 CanLII 2625 (BC CA)
, 16 B.C.L.R. (2d) 98 (C.A.), where a claim of a duty to warn was held an
appropriate extension of a claim in negligence.  Here, it is the opposite
situation.  The writ alleges a duty to warn but the claim advanced in the
statement of claim is in negligence.

[
37
]

In
Rotvold v. Rocky Mountain Diesel Ltd.
(1994),
100 B.C.L.R. (2d) 391 (S.C.)
, Melnick J. discussed Rule 20(3).  The question
before Melnick J. was whether allegations of fraud and misrepresentation were
new causes of action and barred by the
Limitation Act
or simply
elaborations on the causes of action in the writ.  The endorsement on the writ
claimed damages for wrongful seizure of a vehicle, damages for wrongful
dismissal, and damages for breach of contract, and the paragraph said to give
rise to new causes of action in the statement of claim alleged fraud and/or
misrepresentation with respect to a lease.  Melnick J. reviewed the relevant
authorities and indicated that earlier cases suggested a broad approach to the
interpretation of what is now Rule 20(3):
MacKenzie v. Schluter
(1967),

1967 CanLII 552 (BC CA)
, 62 W.W.R. 291.  He said at ¶24: “The allegations of fraud and misrepresentation
are simply part of Mr. Rotvold's account of the way in which the agreements
were made.  They are not independent of the contractual matters that are
referred to in the writ of summons.”

[
38
]

The defendants rely on
McFarlane v.
Holmberg
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 167 (S.C.)
where the inclusion of a
paragraph in the statement of claim had the effect of “setting up a new cause
of action against the defendants or individuals who are not now defendants”;
Master Doolan concluded that “such claims, being statute barred, must be
struck”.  Here, there is already an existing claim in the pleadings against the
particular defendants.

[
39
]

Given the broad approach to Rule 20(3) mentioned
in
Rotvold
, I consider the claim here in negligence to be
sufficiently related to the claim of a duty to warn that I think it is a
permissible pleading under Rule 20(3).  The claim in the writ of summons was
not simply a breach of a duty to warn of construction deficiencies, which were
defined in the writ of summons as defects in the workmanship, materials and
design; the writ also alleged –  although not initially against the Kwans –
negligence and a breach of duty of care.  The statement of claim then extended
the breach of duty of care claim to the individual Kwans, and alleged that the
Kwans’ breach of duty contributed to the construction deficiencies.

DECISION

[
40
]

I allow the amendments as it is not plain and
obvious that they do not disclose a reasonable cause of action.

[
41
]

In exercising my discretion to grant the
amendments, given the argument that there has been an intervening limitation
period, I consider that the negligence claim in the statement of claim is a
permissible extension of the writ, without amending the endorsement.
Therefore, the amendments that I allow are in substance particulars of the duty
and standard of care in connection with the negligence plea that appears in the
statement of claim.

[
42
]

On the other hand, if I am wrong and the plea of
negligence in the statement of claim is not permissible under Rule 20(3), I
would nevertheless exercise my discretion to allow the amendment.  The Kwans
have been aware of the claim against them in negligence since the original
statement of claim.  They denied any duty of care was owed by them in their
statement of defence, dated June 15, 2006.  They are defendants and are
principals of the contractor.  Given the fact that the claim in negligence was
advanced when the statement of claim was filed, I am unable to identify any
significant delay or prejudice and none was described to me.

[
43
]

Accordingly, the proposed amendments are
allowed.

“J.S. Sigurdson J.”

The
Honourable Mr. Justice J.S. Sigurdson
